text:
If two of your strongest engineers are in friction, and you let it run through another quarter of quiet standoffs, the whole team will pay for it. Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 teams and found that psychological safety mattered more than who was on the team.

Don't referee personalities. Referee interfaces, meaning the points where one person's work depends on the other's. Most feuds between senior engineers are really disputes over who has design authority, even though they look like grudges. A document that sets out ownership boundaries and names who decides what usually drains much of the heat.

Meet each engineer separately first. You'll likely find that each believes the other is slowing delivery. Then schedule a joint session with a written agenda and one shared, measurable deliverable.

Tuckman's 1965 model calls this stage "storming", and teams that skip it rarely reach "performing". Watch the comment threads on code reviews, because tone shows up there before anyone resigns. If one of them threatens to leave, remember that replacing a senior engineer often costs six to nine months of salary.

Mediate early, or you may have to cut someone loose later.
